I'll take the liberty of starting a new topic for analysis of the actual project code so that the existing topic can remain focused on the high-level discussions.

I started an exploration of optimizing the elaboration of an initial cone of 100 FLT modules on Mastodon: https://functional.cafe/@kha/117217723466719828. To cut to the chase, this is the current state.

I think that manipulation of the code, now it exists, is something well worth thinking about. For example people have asked what fragment of mathematics is necessary for a full proof of FLT and surely the repo gives some way of being able to explore this question (although there will still be plenty of difficult problems to solve here). I have already been asked how much axiom-of-choice has been used in the proof, and Lean is not designed to answer that question (AC is everywhere), but now we have the code it might be possible to try and answer this.

I found it quite difficult navigating my way around the codebase in its current state in VS Code, even after having got everything compiled, simply because it was so large. It will be interesting to see what effect modulizing has on it.
Nice, very cool Sebastian Ullrich.

Tianyi, who led most of the actual work, has uploaded the HTML "guide" to a GitHub pages that he hosts here. This is in the original GitHub but wasn't hosted before. It has a lot of detail about the Prove2Me DAG and how the theorem is constructed

One more update from me for today: using the same recipe as above, Fable was able to extend it to 1000 modules (S_ModularCurve_PlaceSpecialization_red_eq_zero_of_isCuspidal_of_coeffEmb_modularUnitSeries_inv_sub_algebraMap_mem_nonunits) mostly by itself

@Sebastian Ullrich this is great! Do you have a general skill for that, or a clear md somewhere. This should be useful for other developments too.
Im currently migrating my computational crypto library to a new lean version, and its quite slow.
I've used some of these techniques, but you seems to have a very nice toolbox for them.

@Bas Spitters The specific steps are all about how to deal with the Prove2Me structure, otherwise it's "use Modulize" and "use shake". I believe it is accumulating a good bit of knowledge about how to fix module system failures in the code but I don't know how translatable that is to other projects.

One thing you could try is to try to upload a simplified proof of FLT on prove2me -- https://prove2.me/missions/Fermat%20Last%20Theorem/graph -- or would these improvements need to happen in prove2me's lean compilation scheme?
This is very cool thanks @Sebastian Ullrich!
